problem.title: Tokenized stocks are easy to buy and hard to hold.
problem.lede: Shares settle on Solana in a second. Keeping them safe afterwards still asks the holder to do four things no holder should have to do.

slides.title: Custody you do not control
slides.body: Left on an exchange, a tokenized share is a claim on a company that holds the keys, and that can freeze, delist or lose it while the market is open. Self-custody is the whole point of putting a stock on chain.
slides.alt: Shares held inside an exchange account, behind a lock the holder does not own

slides.title: You approve a string you cannot read
slides.body: A hardware wallet shows a hash and asks for a confirmation. A swapped destination account, a hidden extra leg or a wrong amount look exactly like a correct order at that size.
slides.alt: A wallet screen showing a hexadecimal hash above an approve button

slides.title: A gas token you never wanted
slides.body: Buying one tokenized share starts with buying SOL, keeping SOL, and topping SOL up for account rent. A long-term holder should not have to run a fee balance in a second asset.
slides.alt: A stock purchase blocked behind an empty fee balance

slides.title: Nothing checks the price
slides.body: No wallet compares the order to the market. A stale quote, a sandwich or a bad route is signed exactly as fast as a fair one, and the signature is final.
slides.alt: An order signed at a price far away from the market price

proofs.eyebrow: Core mechanic | what the phone does
proofs.title: Three things your wallet does not do today.
proofs.lede: All three run on a device in airplane mode, with no network, no fee token and no trust in the machine showing the QR.

cards.title: Zero-SOL cold storage
cards.goal: The signing device never holds a fee token, and never needs one.
bullets: The vault account signs the swap and nothing else
A PixStock relayer is the fee payer and pays the rent for new token accounts
Nothing on the phone has to be funded, topped up or bridged
The policy refuses any message where the vault is the fee payer
cards.block: fee payer and signer are separate accounts at the protocol level, and durable nonces are built for signing offline. No workaround required.

cards.title: It shows the order, not a hash
cards.goal: The phone decompiles the transaction itself and prints a ticket a human can check.
bullets: Every instruction decoded offline: program, accounts, amounts
Destination token accounts derived on device and matched to your vault
Ten policy rules run before the ticket is even shown
Anything it cannot decode is refused, never approved quietly
cards.block: sell 250.00 USDC, receive at least 0.812 TSLAx, into an account the phone derived itself. Nothing else fits in the message.

cards.title: It checks the price offline
cards.goal: A signed Pyth message travels with the order, and the phone verifies it with no network at all.
bullets: Ed25519 signature and signer set verified on device
Message age checked against the order it came with
Implied price of the swap compared to the attested price
More than 1 % of drift and the phone refuses to sign
cards.block: a hardware wallet cannot tell a fair route from a sandwich. This one can, in airplane mode, in about 145 bytes of signed price.

pieces.eyebrow: Two more, while we are here
pieces.title: A basket in one scan. A backup you can print.
pieces.lede: The optical channel is not a toy: it carries a full three-leg basket, and it carries the key itself when you need a backup.

basket.title: Three stocks, one signature
basket.claim: An equal-weight basket of AAPLx, NVDAx and MSFTx routes through Jupiter inside a single transaction of 910 bytes, measured rather than estimated, and crosses the air gap in five frames. Solana's limit is 1,232, and the number moves with the route Jupiter picks.
basket.note: Versioned transactions and address lookup tables keep the whole allocation inside one message, so one scan and one approval settle all three positions.

paper.title: A vault you can print
paper.claim: The key is sealed with AES-GCM-256 behind an Argon2id password and exported as a QR you print on one sheet. Restore it on any offline device; nothing is ever stored with us.
paper.note: The decrypted key exists only in memory, and is zeroed as soon as the signature is produced. The encrypted blob never leaves the device except as that sheet of paper.

flow.title: Four steps. The key crosses nothing but light.
flow.lede: The browser never sees a key, the phone never sees a network, and the two only ever exchange pictures.

steps.d: Pick a stock or a basket on the web app. The order and its signed Pyth price are packed into AGQP frames.
The browser plays the frames as an animated QR at 8 fps. The phone reads them with its camera, still in airplane mode.
The phone reassembles the order, checks the attested price and every signing rule, and prints the ticket for you to read.
Biometric approval, signature back by QR to the webcam. The relayer pays the fee and broadcasts. Solscan link in about a second.

phases: Air-gapped · the key never leaves the phone

objections.title: The four questions everyone asks first.

items.q: Do I need SOL to use this?
items.a: No. The relayer is the fee payer and also pays the rent for any token account your order has to open. The vault holds no SOL, ever, and the relayer can only pay: it has no authority over anything you own.

items.q: What if the relayer goes down or censors me?
items.a: The transaction is already signed and built on a durable nonce, so any RPC and any other fee payer can broadcast it. The relayer is a convenience with a public policy, not a dependency.

items.q: Why not just buy a hardware wallet?
items.a: Buy one if you want. It will still show you a hash, still ask you for a fee token, and still have no idea whether the price you are signing is the market price. A spare phone in airplane mode costs nothing and fixes all three.
No. The vault app makes no network calls at all. Its headers ship connect-src 'none', so you can verify that yourself in the inspector, and the only channel in or out is the camera and the screen.

cta.lede: Open the vault on a spare phone, turn airplane mode on, and run a devnet order end to end. Nothing to install, nothing to fund.

meta.title: The protocol
meta.ogTitle: PixStock | AGQP, the signing policy and the offline price guard
meta.description: How an order crosses an air gap as animated QR codes, what the phone checks before it signs, and why a corrupted browser cannot lie to it about the price.

pageHead.title: How an order crosses the gap
pageHead.lede: No cable, no radio, no pairing. A laptop shows animated QR codes, a phone reads them with its camera, and sixty-four bytes of signature come back the same way.

channel.title: The optical channel
body: A Solana transaction, the price attestation that guards it and a readable description of the order add up to more than one QR code can hold. AGQP splits them into indexed frames that cycle on screen forever, so the phone can join the sequence at any point and a frame it missed comes back on the next pass. Nothing is timed and nothing is clicked.

Each frame carries a CRC of its own chunk. QR codes already carry Reed-Solomon correction, so a frame either decodes or it does not; the CRC covers what happens after, when the bytes are reassembled. A corrupted frame is dropped in silence and the cycle reissues it.

Frames are Base45, the encoding behind EU digital certificates. The browser API that reads a QR hands back a string, not bytes, so raw binary would be mangled in transit. Base45 costs about three percent over raw bytes, against thirty-three for Base64, and keeps every frame inside the QR alphanumeric character set, which is what keeps the codes small enough to read across a desk.

fields.magic: Protocol marker. Anything else is ignored without a sound.
fields.sid: Session id. The phone locks onto the first valid frame and ignores every other session after that.
fields.counters: Position and count, up to {max} frames.
fields.crc: Integrity of this chunk, uppercase hex.
fields.chunk: A slice of the payload, Base45.

channel.sizes: The header is {header} characters. The frame size is adjustable: {s}, {m} or {l} bytes per frame. Screen contrast, camera quality and distance all move the optimum, and the right setting is the one measured on the phone in the room. At {fps} frames per second, a five-frame order cycles in well under a second.

policy.title: What the phone checks before it signs
body: A hardware wallet that shows you a hash is asking you to trust the screen that produced it. The phone decompiles the transaction itself: it reads the accounts, names the programs, pulls the amounts out of the swap instruction and derives your own token accounts to confirm the output is really coming to you.

The order description that travels alongside is never the source of truth. Every figure shown to you comes from the decompiled instructions; the description is only ever compared against them, and a disagreement is a refusal, not a warning.
policy.honesty: A rule that is not implemented is not a rule that passes. While {unevaluated} is unenforced the policy refuses to return a clean verdict at all, and says which rule is missing. A green tick that skipped a check is worse than no tick.
policy.allEnforced: Every rule in this table is evaluated on the phone, and the policy returns a clean verdict only when all of them pass. The result carries the list it checked, so a rule that was ever removed would show as missing rather than silently stop applying. A green tick that skipped a check is worse than no tick.
policy.cap: Slippage is capped at {cap} basis points in the phone itself, whatever an order asks for.

pyth.title: The offline price guard
body: This is the part no hardware wallet does today. A signed price message from Pyth travels with the order, and the phone verifies its Ed25519 signature against trusted keys it already holds, with no network, in a few milliseconds.

If the order's implied price drifts more than one percent from the signed one, the phone refuses to sign and says why. A browser that has been tampered with can show you any number it likes; it cannot forge a signature from an oracle whose keys are already on your phone.
The guard degrades honestly. If no attested price is available, the order ticket says the price is unattested rather than quietly signing anyway.
pyth.status: Built and enforced. The vault parses Pyth's signed message, checks its Ed25519 signature against the keys Pyth publishes on chain, and refuses to sign past one percent, all offline. One limit, stated plainly: our Pyth grant currently covers the Tesla feed, so a basket of the other four travels with a price for the legs it covers and the ticket names the ones it does not.

paperVault.title: Paper-Vault
body: Your key is encrypted with AES-GCM-256 under a key derived from your master password with Argon2id, and the whole record fits in a single QR code you print on one sheet: parameters, salt, nonce, ciphertext and public key.

The cost parameters are stored inside the record, so raising them later never orphans a backup printed today. Paper alone cannot spend: without the password it is an encrypted blob, and nothing about it ever touches a cloud.

sections.title: Tokenized stocks are not available everywhere
body: The xStocks referenced here are issued by Backed Finance. They are not offered to US, UK, Canadian or Australian persons, and eligibility rules elsewhere vary by jurisdiction. PixStock does not issue, custody or redeem them, and being able to load this page is not a statement that you are eligible to hold them.
Determining your own eligibility is your responsibility. If you are unsure, do not proceed.

sections.title: The issuer can seize or freeze these tokens
body: Every xStock referenced here is a Token-2022 mint with a permanent delegate and a freeze authority, both held by the issuer. Verified on mainnet: all five share the delegate 5aMNNLQJwAEeoemTEMkv5NVjqKwvvefRYCQ5Z67HFvEq. That address can move tokens out of any account holding them, including yours, without your signature. The freeze authority can make an account unusable.

This is how a regulated issuer meets its obligations, and it is not something PixStock can change. It is also the honest limit of what an air-gapped signer protects: it stops anyone who is not the issuer from moving your assets, and it cannot stop the issuer.
Solana surfaces it too. Creating an account for one of these mints logs "Mint has a permanent delegate, so tokens in this account may be seized at any time".

sections.title: Nothing here is investment advice
body: PixStock is signing infrastructure. It does not recommend assets, it does not construct portfolios for you, and the basket presets are illustrations of a mechanism, not suggestions. No part of this site is a recommendation to buy, sell or hold anything.
Prices shown come from third-party sources. Tokenized equities can lose value, can trade away from the underlying, and can become illiquid.

sections.title: This is a demonstration
body: PixStock was built for the Stocklana hackathon and is early software. It has not been audited. Parts of the signing policy are not yet enforced, and the interface says so where that is the case.
Use amounts you are willing to lose entirely, and prefer a devnet vault for anything exploratory.

sections.title: Keys and custody
body: PixStock never transmits, stores or has access to your private key. It is generated on your device, encrypted with your master password, and stays there. Nobody, including us, can recover it if you lose that password.
No PixStock contributor or process will ever ask for your seed phrase, your master password or your private key. Any message that does is fraudulent.

pageHead.title: Pair your offline signer
pageHead.lede: Open the vault on a phone in airplane mode and show its pairing code to this webcam. This page learns a public key and nothing else.

pairing.title: Pairing
pairing.body: The vault displays a code holding its public key, a label and the network it is set to. Scanning it teaches this browser where to send orders and whose balances to show. It carries no secret, so a photograph of it is harmless.
pairing.manualSummary: No webcam on this machine? Type the address instead
pairing.manualBody: The vault prints its address under the code, on the same screen. Typing it reaches the same place the scan does: a public key this browser remembers, and nothing else. Check the first and last four characters against the phone before you build an order against it.

pending.title: Hold the vault's code up to the webcam
pending.body: On the phone, tap "Show my address" and point it at this camera. The scanner reads the pairing record and remembers where to send orders. Anything else you hold up is named rather than accepted. A Paper-Vault backup belongs on paper, never in a browser.

watchOnly.title: Watch-only, by construction
watchOnly.body: Nothing on this page can move an asset. It shows balances and order history; every instruction that spends is signed on the phone, and the phone is the only thing that holds a key.
